proposition: UCSF policy assigns patient accommodation responsibility to treating clinical care department/inpatient unit and/or Patient Relations.
UCSF policy provides financial escalation paths for qualifying accommodation/barrier-removal work.
UCSF publicly states patients may complain without compromising quality or future access to care.
Patient Relations and care-team/accessibility routes are published for unresolved concerns and accommodations.
The patient requests direct verifiable routing to independent institutional functions.
Published routes do not prove patient-specific receipt, review, assignment or completion.
A local workload reduction can shift work to another UCSF function or to the patient rather than reduce total work.
Test a single coordinating entry point that identifies distinct accepted owners without making one person perform every function.
Record or portal presence alone does not establish review, understanding or agreement absent evidence or a governing rule.
Actual decision provenance, routing, case identifiers and delivered accommodation remain open.
Regents hold University governance authority and delegate operations subject to reserved powers.
Chancellors are responsible for campus organization, administration, operations and financial management within University policy/budget.
The Health Services Committee has strategic direction and oversight concerning UC Health.
BUS-10 requires clear financial-accountability lines and qualified/authorized delegation.
These governance sources do not establish that UCOP, Regents, HSC or the Chancellor reviewed this patient's matter.
BUS-10 is a financial-transaction accountability policy, not a general clinical standard of care.
System scale can reduce or increase coordination cost depending on actual delegation; affiliation alone establishes neither.
Escalate to UC-level authority only when policy/delegation actually assigns a system role.
Copying a UC-level office does not establish review or responsibility without routing and authority evidence.
Actual UC system involvement in the patient-specific decisions remains unestablished.
The Medical Board licenses/regulates physicians, screens complaints, investigates and disciplines within its jurisdiction.
Board complaint stages distinguish screening, investigation, lesser enforcement, Attorney General referral and discipline.
The Board states it cannot provide medical care or malpractice compensation.
Complaint receipt, investigation or referral is not an adjudicated violation.
Regulatory investigation can reduce information asymmetry but also consumes public, professional and patient resources.
Keep professional-regulation work parallel to care/access rather than making regulatory completion a condition of treatment.
A filed complaint does not establish a disciplinary finding; each process state remains distinct.
Complaint status, timeliness, evidence and disposition remain case-specific and unresolved here.
CRD enforces covered civil-rights laws for state-funded programs and investigates qualifying complaints.
CDPH/CHCQ regulates health-care facilities/providers within its licensing/certification purview and investigates complaints.
California is not one centralized health-care dispute office; agency jurisdictions remain distinct.
Receipt or jurisdictional acceptance by one state agency does not establish merits or notice to another agency.
Jurisdictional fragmentation can create transaction costs without itself proving illegality.
Identify the correct forum once per proposition and preserve routing evidence to reduce repetitive jurisdiction work.
Coverage, event-date law, deadlines, exhaustion and remedies remain proposition-specific.
Use the ten-state notice ladder bidirectionally; do not promote record presence into review, understanding or agreement without support.
Assign responsibility only from actual authority, not affiliation or rhetorical severity.
Keep internal work, shifted labor, duplication, delay, lived loss and damages as different cost categories.
Visible ownership, limits and handoffs can reduce coordination burden; whether a particular failure was avoidable requires evidence.
Framework completion does not equal patient-specific application, whole-book evidence completion or manuscript acceptance.
